opening.text: Imagine you are on a long hike. Someone hands you a stone at the trailhead. It is small. You put it in your backpack and keep walking.

A mile later, someone else hands you a stone. You take it too. Then another. Some of them you picked up yourself, because you were angry and you wanted proof. After a few hours, your shoulders ache. Your steps get slow. You start to wonder why the trail feels so hard.
The trail is not the problem. The weight is.

That is what an unforgiven hurt does to us. It does not stay small. It rides along with us, day after day. We carry it into our homes, our wards, and our prayers. And the person who hurt us often has no idea we are still carrying it.
Today I want to talk about putting the stones down. I want to talk about forgiveness. Not as a rule that makes life harder, but as a gift that makes the climb lighter.

I will speak about two kinds of forgiveness. The first is the forgiveness God gives us. The second is the forgiveness He asks us to give to others. They are tied together. And once we see how, the whole thing starts to make sense.

mainMessage.text: Forgiveness comes from Jesus Christ. He forgives us fully, and He asks us to forgive others. When we do, He lifts the weight from our hearts and gives us peace.

blocks.text: Let's start with how God sees us.

Many people think of God as a judge with a long list of our mistakes. The scriptures paint a different picture. They show a Father who is patient and slow to get angry. A Father who would rather forgive than remember.
The psalmist describes Him this way.

The Lord is merciful and gracious, slow to anger, and plenteous in mercy. He will not always chide: neither will he keep his anger for ever. He hath not dealt with us after our sins; nor rewarded us according to our iniquities. For as the heaven is high above the earth, so great is his mercy toward them that fear him. As far as the east is from the west, so far hath he removed our transgressions from us.
Look at that last image. East and west never meet. You can walk east your whole life and you will never end up in the west. That is how far God puts our sins from us when He forgives.
Now, how do we receive that? John gives a clear answer.
If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.
The word is faithful. God keeps His word. If we come to Him honestly, He does not turn us away. He forgives, and He cleans.
And Isaiah records the Lord's own voice on this.
I, even I, am he that blotteth out thy transgressions for mine own sake, and will not remember thy sins.
The Lord says, I will not remember. That is hard for us to picture. We remember everything. But He says He will let it go.

So here is the first truth. God's forgiveness is real, and it is complete. If you have been afraid that He is still holding something against you, hear these words again. He is merciful. He is faithful. He does not keep a record to use against you.
Now, how can God forgive us and still be just? The answer is Jesus Christ.

Sin has a cost. Someone has to pay it. Jesus took that cost on Himself. He suffered in Gethsemane and on the cross so that we would not have to carry the full weight of our sins alone. Paul puts it simply.
In whom we have redemption through his blood, even the forgiveness of sins.
Forgiveness is not cheap. It cost the Savior everything. That is why we do not take it lightly. And it is also why we can trust it. It was paid for in full.
The Book of Mormon repeats the promise many times. The Lord speaks to Alma and says this.
Yea, and as often as my people repent will I forgive them their trespasses against me.
As often as. Not once. Not twice. As often as we repent. That does not mean we should be careless. It means we should never give up and think we have used up His patience.
Elder Russell M. Nelson once taught about the meaning of the word atonement. In his talk "The Atonement," from the October 1996 general conference, he said:

Rich meaning is found in study of the word atonement in the Semitic languages of Old Testament times. In Hebrew, the basic word for atonement is kaphar, a verb that means “to cover” or “to forgive.” Closely related is the Aramaic and Arabic word kafat, meaning “a close embrace”—no doubt related to the Egyptian ritual embrace. References to that embrace are evident in the Book of Mormon. One states that “the Lord hath redeemed my soul . . . ; I have beheld his glory, and I am encircled about eternally in the arms of his love.” \[2 Nephi 1:15.\] Another proffers the glorious hope of our being “clasped in the arms of Jesus.” \[Mormon 5:11.\]
I love that. The word for atonement is close to the word for an embrace. Forgiveness is not only a cleared record. It is being held.
Lehi felt that when he spoke to his sons.
But behold, the Lord hath redeemed my soul from hell; I have beheld his glory, and I am encircled about eternally in the arms of his love.
So the second truth is this. Forgiveness is possible because of Jesus Christ. And He does not forgive from a distance. He forgives with open arms.
Here is where it gets personal. The same Savior who forgives us asks us to forgive others.
He was very plain about this. In the Sermon on the Mount, He said:
For if ye forgive men their trespasses, your heavenly Father will also forgive you: But if ye forgive not men their trespasses, neither will your Father forgive your trespasses.
That is a serious statement. And it can feel unfair at first. Why would God tie His forgiveness of me to how I treat someone else?
Here is one way to see it. If my hands are clenched around a grudge, I cannot receive anything. I have no open hand. Forgiving others is not payment for God's mercy. It is how we make room for it.
In our day, the Lord repeated the command and made it even stronger.

Wherefore, I say unto you, that ye ought to forgive one another; for he that forgiveth not his brother his trespasses standeth condemned before the Lord; for there remaineth in him the greater sin. I, the Lord, will forgive whom I will forgive, but of you it is required to forgive all men. And ye ought to say in your hearts—let God judge between me and thee, and reward thee according to thy deeds.
Notice the last part. Let God judge. We are not asked to decide what the other person deserves. We are asked to hand that job to Someone who sees everything and who is perfectly fair.
President Gordon B. Hinckley knew that this is not easy. In his article "Of You It Is Required to Forgive," in the June 1991 Ensign, he wrote:
I plead with you to ask the Lord for strength to forgive. . . . It may not be easy, and it may not come quickly. But if you will seek it with sincerity and cultivate it, it will come.

I find comfort in that. He does not say it will be easy. He does not say it will be fast. He says, ask for strength, and keep at it. If forgiving someone feels impossible today, you are not failing. You are in the middle of the work.
So how do we actually put the stones down? Let's get practical.
The first step is to be honest about what we feel. Many of us hide anger from ourselves. We say, "It's fine," when it is not fine. But a stone you will not look at is a stone you cannot drop.
President James E. Faust gave this advice in his talk "The Healing Power of Forgiveness," from the April 2007 general conference:

We need to recognize and acknowledge angry feelings. It will take humility to do this, but if we will get on our knees and ask Heavenly Father for a feeling of forgiveness, He will help us. The Lord requires us “to forgive all men” \[D&C 64:10\] for our own good because “hatred retards spiritual growth.” \[Orson F. Whitney, Gospel Themes (1914), 144.\] Only as we rid ourselves of hatred and bitterness can the Lord put comfort into our hearts. . . .

Notice what he says. Name the feeling. Then kneel and ask for help. We do not have to find the strength alone. And notice the reason. The Lord asks us to forgive for our own good. This is not a rule made to burden us. It is a rule made to protect us.
The second step is to see how Christ forgave. Paul gives us the pattern.
Forbearing one another, and forgiving one another, if any man have a quarrel against any: even as Christ forgave you, so also do ye.
Even as Christ forgave you. That is the measure. Not as the world forgives, with conditions and a long memory. As Christ forgave.
The third step is to let go of the role of judge. Jesus said:
Judge not, and ye shall not be judged: condemn not, and ye shall not be condemned: forgive, and ye shall be forgiven.
When we forgive, we do not say what happened was fine. We say, I will not be the one to hand out the sentence. I leave that with God.
And the highest example of all came from the cross. Hanging there in pain, after being mocked and beaten, Jesus said this.
Then said Jesus, Father, forgive them; for they know not what they do. And they parted his raiment, and cast lots.
He was still in agony. He did not wait for an apology. He forgave first.
President Faust added a second thought that matters when the hurt is deep. He said:

. . . When tragedy strikes, we should not respond by seeking personal revenge but rather let justice take its course and then let go. It is not easy to let go and empty our hearts of festering resentment. The Savior has offered to all of us a precious peace through His Atonement, but this can come only as we are willing to cast out negative feelings of anger, spite, or revenge.

Let justice take its course. Forgiving does not mean we stay in harm's way. It does not mean we ignore wrongs that the law or the Church must handle. It means that once those things are in the right hands, we stop carrying the anger ourselves.
Now I want to speak to the person who thinks, "I could forgive others. But I cannot believe God has forgiven me."

Some of you carry a heavy stone of your own. You did something, years ago maybe, and you still wince when you think of it. You have prayed. You have changed. And still a voice says, "That is too big."

Let's look at someone who had every reason to believe that. The people of Ammon were Lamanites who had done terrible things. They had killed. When they came to the Lord, this is how one of their leaders prayed.

And I also thank my God, yea, my great God, that he hath granted unto us that we might repent of these things, and also that he hath forgiven us of those our many sins and murders which we have committed, and taken away the guilt from our hearts, through the merits of his Son.
He said it plainly. He forgave us. He took away the guilt from our hearts. Notice that the guilt itself was lifted. Not just covered up, not just ignored.
President Boyd K. Packer spoke about this in his talk "The Brilliant Morning of Forgiveness," from the October 1995 general conference. He said:

The gospel teaches us that relief from torment and guilt can be earned through repentance. Save for those few who defect to perdition after having known a fulness, there is no habit, no addiction, no rebellion, no transgression, no offense exempted from the promise of complete forgiveness.
No habit. No addiction. No rebellion. No transgression. No offense. That list covers a lot of ground. Whatever you are carrying, it is on that list.
Elder Neil L. Andersen said it this way in his talk "Repent . . . That I May Heal You," from the October 2009 general conference:

I testify that the Savior is able and eager to forgive our sins. Except for the sins of those few who choose perdition after having known a fulness, there is no sin that cannot be forgiven. What a marvelous privilege for each of us to turn away from our sins and to come unto Christ. Divine forgiveness is one of the sweetest fruits of the gospel, removing guilt and pain from our hearts and replacing them with joy and peace of conscience.
Able and eager. Not just able. Eager. He wants to forgive you. If you take only one line home today, take that one.
Finally, forgiveness is not a one-time event. It is a way of living.
Peter asked the Lord a question many of us have asked quietly.

Then came Peter to him, and said, Lord, how oft shall my brother sin against me, and I forgive him? till seven times? Jesus saith unto him, I say not unto thee, Until seven times: but, Until seventy times seven.
Peter thought seven was generous. Jesus answered with a number so large it stops being a number. It becomes a habit. We forgive, and when the hurt comes back, we forgive again.
What does that look like day to day? Paul tells us.

Let all bitterness, and wrath, and anger, and clamour, and evil speaking, be put away from you, with all malice: And be ye kind one to another, tenderhearted, forgiving one another, even as God for Christ's sake hath forgiven you.

Put away. Be kind. Be tenderhearted. These are small choices. We make them at the dinner table, in the car, in the group chat. A softer answer. A word we decide not to say. A good thought about someone who has not earned it.
That is how the backpack gets lighter. Not in one dramatic moment, but one stone at a time.

story.prompt: The member tells a true time when they forgave someone, or when someone forgave them. If the member has none, the app offers a story from the scriptures.
story.title: Joseph forgives his brothers

blocks.text: Joseph's brothers sold him into slavery. He lost his home, his father, and years of his life. Later he became a ruler in Egypt, and the same brothers came to him in need. After their father died, they were afraid. They thought Joseph would finally take revenge. This is what he said to them.

And Joseph said unto them, Fear not: for am I in the place of God? But as for you, ye thought evil against me; but God meant it unto good, to bring to pass, as it is this day, to save much people alive. Now therefore fear ye not: I will nourish you, and your little ones. And he comforted them, and spake kindly unto them.
Joseph did not pretend it did not hurt. He said, "ye thought evil against me." But he let go of the judge's seat. He asked, "am I in the place of God?" Then he fed them, and he spoke kindly to them.

application.text: This week, try one small thing.
Take a quiet moment and ask yourself, "What stone am I carrying?" Write down the name or the memory. Do not judge yourself for it.
Then kneel and ask Heavenly Father for the feeling of forgiveness. Ask Him to help you want it, if you do not yet. That is enough for day one.
If the stone is about someone else, pray for that person by name for a week. It is hard to hold a grudge against someone you pray for.
If the stone is about you, read 1 John 1:9 again. Then confess to the Lord, and if the matter is serious, speak with your bishop or branch president. Let Christ lift it.

testimony.prompt: The member adds their own words. Lines the app offers:

blocks.text: I know that Jesus Christ forgives. I have felt the weight of things I carried, and I have felt it lift. I know that He asks us to forgive others, and I know that He gives us the strength to do it. When we put our stones down, we find peace we could not make on our own. I say these things in the name of Jesus Christ, amen.

invitations: I invite you to ask yourself, "What stone am I carrying?" and write it down.
I invite you to ask Heavenly Father for the feeling of forgiveness, and pray for the person by name.
I invite you to confess to the Lord, and speak with your bishop or branch president if the matter is serious.
blessings: You will be cleansed through Jesus Christ.

closingVerse.text: Come now, and let us reason together, saith the Lord: though your sins be as scarlet, they shall be as white as snow; though they be red like crimson, they shall be as wool.

opening.text: There is an old saying about anger. Holding a grudge is like grabbing a hot coal to throw at someone. You plan to burn them. But you are the one who gets burned.

I have seen it happen. A family stops speaking at holidays. Two friends cross the street to avoid each other. A man sits in church every Sunday and cannot look at the person three rows ahead. Years pass. The person who caused the hurt has moved on. And the coal is still in the hand of the one who was hurt.
We do not usually call it a burn. We call it being right. We say, "I have every reason to be upset." And often that is true. The hurt was real.
But being right is a heavy thing to hold. And the Lord offers us something better than being right. He offers us peace.
Today I want to talk about how to open the hand. We will look at what God does with our sins, what He asks us to do with the sins of others, and why those two things belong together.

mainMessage.text: When we forgive, we follow the Savior and we free ourselves. He forgave us at great cost, and He teaches us to pass that mercy on. Through Him, our hearts can heal.

blocks.text: Before we talk about what we owe others, let's start with what we have been given.
If you ever worry that God is quick to anger or slow to forgive, the Psalms say the opposite. Listen to how David describes the Lord.

The Lord is merciful and gracious, slow to anger, and plenteous in mercy. He will not always chide: neither will he keep his anger for ever. He hath not dealt with us after our sins; nor rewarded us according to our iniquities. For as the heaven is high above the earth, so great is his mercy toward them that fear him. As far as the east is from the west, so far hath he removed our transgressions from us.

Picture the sky. It has no ceiling you can touch. That is how big His mercy is. Then picture the distance from east to west. There is no end to it. That is how far our sins are moved when He forgives.
There is a condition, and it is gentle. We come to Him and tell the truth.
If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.
He is faithful. That means we can count on Him. We do not have to wonder each time whether He will keep His promise.
And He tells us what He does with what He forgives.
I, even I, am he that blotteth out thy transgressions for mine own sake, and will not remember thy sins.
When we forgive, we often say, "I forgive, but I will never forget." The Lord says something different about Himself. He does not hold on to the memory in order to use it later.

This matters for what comes next. We can only give away what we have received. If you do not believe you are forgiven, it is very hard to forgive anyone else. So let that truth settle in first. You are not a file of old mistakes to Him. You are a child He wants to bring home.
Why is God able to forgive so freely? Because Someone already paid.
Think about what forgiveness is. When someone wrongs you and you forgive them, you take the loss on yourself. You say, "You owe me, but I will not collect." That costs you something.
Now think about the Savior. Every sin has a cost, and He took all of those costs on Himself. Paul wrote:
In whom we have redemption through his blood, even the forgiveness of sins.
Redemption means to buy back. He bought us back. That is why His forgiveness is not a loophole. It is a gift with a price attached, and He paid it.
Then He made a promise to the people of Alma, and it applies to us.
Yea, and as often as my people repent will I forgive them their trespasses against me.

Think of how many times you have gone back to Him with the same struggle. Maybe you felt embarrassed. Maybe you wondered if He was tired of you. This verse answers that. As often as. Each time we return, He receives us.
Elder Russell M. Nelson gave us a beautiful picture of what this forgiveness feels like. In his October 1996 general conference talk, "The Atonement," he explained:

Rich meaning is found in study of the word atonement in the Semitic languages of Old Testament times. In Hebrew, the basic word for atonement is kaphar, a verb that means “to cover” or “to forgive.” Closely related is the Aramaic and Arabic word kafat, meaning “a close embrace”—no doubt related to the Egyptian ritual embrace. References to that embrace are evident in the Book of Mormon. One states that “the Lord hath redeemed my soul . . . ; I have beheld his glory, and I am encircled about eternally in the arms of his love.” \[2 Nephi 1:15.\] Another proffers the glorious hope of our being “clasped in the arms of Jesus.” \[Mormon 5:11.\]
To cover. To embrace. To be clasped in His arms. This is not the language of a courtroom. It is the language of a father running down the road to meet his child.
The prophet Lehi used those same words near the end of his life.
But behold, the Lord hath redeemed my soul from hell; I have beheld his glory, and I am encircled about eternally in the arms of his love.
If you have felt that love, even once, you know why people are willing to forgive. You have been on the receiving end, and it changes you.
Now we come to the part that many of us would like to skip. The Lord asks us to pass this mercy on.
He did not hide it in a footnote. He said it in the Sermon on the Mount, right after teaching the Lord's Prayer.
For if ye forgive men their trespasses, your heavenly Father will also forgive you: But if ye forgive not men their trespasses, neither will your Father forgive your trespasses.

Why such a firm statement? I think it is because a heart cannot be open and closed at the same time. If I am gripping a coal, I cannot take the gift He is holding out. He is not punishing us. He is telling us what our hands are doing.
In a revelation to the early Saints, He said it again, and added something important.

Wherefore, I say unto you, that ye ought to forgive one another; for he that forgiveth not his brother his trespasses standeth condemned before the Lord; for there remaineth in him the greater sin. I, the Lord, will forgive whom I will forgive, but of you it is required to forgive all men. And ye ought to say in your hearts—let God judge between me and thee, and reward thee according to thy deeds.
Two things stand out. First, the Lord reserves the right to decide whom He forgives. He is the judge. We are not. Second, we are asked to forgive everyone. All men. No list of exceptions.
That sounds impossible when the hurt is deep. President Gordon B. Hinckley understood. In his article "Of You It Is Required to Forgive," published in the June 1991 Ensign, he wrote:
I plead with you to ask the Lord for strength to forgive. . . . It may not be easy, and it may not come quickly. But if you will seek it with sincerity and cultivate it, it will come.

He uses the word plead. A prophet pleads with us because he knows how much is at stake. And he gives us permission to take time. It may not come quickly. What he asks is that we keep seeking, honestly, until it does.
Let's talk about the how. When you are holding a hot coal, the first thing you have to admit is that your hand hurts.
That sounds obvious. But many of us skip this step. We tell ourselves we are over it. We keep busy. Then something small happens, and the anger comes rushing back.
President James E. Faust spoke straight to this in his April 2007 general conference talk, "The Healing Power of Forgiveness." He said:

We need to recognize and acknowledge angry feelings. It will take humility to do this, but if we will get on our knees and ask Heavenly Father for a feeling of forgiveness, He will help us. The Lord requires us “to forgive all men” \[D&C 64:10\] for our own good because “hatred retards spiritual growth.” \[Orson F. Whitney, Gospel Themes (1914), 144.\] Only as we rid ourselves of hatred and bitterness can the Lord put comfort into our hearts. . . .

Two things help me here. One, he says it takes humility. Admitting I am angry is not weakness. Two, he says to ask Heavenly Father for a feeling of forgiveness. Not just the act. The feeling. That is a prayer He loves to answer.
Once we are honest, we follow the pattern the Savior set. Paul puts it in one sentence.
Forbearing one another, and forgiving one another, if any man have a quarrel against any: even as Christ forgave you, so also do ye.
Forbearing means putting up with each other. We are all hard to live with at times. Then comes the standard: as Christ forgave.
How did He forgive? He did not first ask for a perfect apology. And He did not first sit as judge. In the Sermon on the Mount, He told us to leave that seat empty.
Judge not, and ye shall not be judged: condemn not, and ye shall not be condemned: forgive, and ye shall be forgiven.
Then He showed us what this looks like when it costs the most.
Then said Jesus, Father, forgive them; for they know not what they do. And they parted his raiment, and cast lots.
The soldiers were dividing His clothes while He suffered. And His prayer was for them.
We may think, "But what if the wrong is serious?" President Faust addressed that too.

. . . When tragedy strikes, we should not respond by seeking personal revenge but rather let justice take its course and then let go. It is not easy to let go and empty our hearts of festering resentment. The Savior has offered to all of us a precious peace through His Atonement, but this can come only as we are willing to cast out negative feelings of anger, spite, or revenge.

See the order. Let justice take its course. Then let go. Forgiveness does not cancel safety, honesty, or the right consequences. It does not mean you must stay close to someone who keeps hurting you. It means you will not let resentment live in you rent free.
Sometimes the hardest person to forgive is not someone else. It is the person in the mirror.
Maybe you made a choice you wish you could undo. You have asked God for forgiveness. Your mind says you are forgiven. Your heart does not catch up. You keep replaying the moment.

If that is you, the scriptures have good news. There is a people in the Book of Mormon who knew this feeling well. The Lamanites who became the people of Ammon had taken many lives before they joined the Church. When they were converted, their king gave thanks to God.

And I also thank my God, yea, my great God, that he hath granted unto us that we might repent of these things, and also that he hath forgiven us of those our many sins and murders which we have committed, and taken away the guilt from our hearts, through the merits of his Son.

The king did not say, "I hope He forgave us." He said, "he hath forgiven us." And the guilt was taken away from their hearts. That is what forgiveness does. It does not only change the record. It changes how we feel inside.
President Boyd K. Packer told us how wide that promise is. In his talk "The Brilliant Morning of Forgiveness," from the October 1995 general conference, he said:

The gospel teaches us that relief from torment and guilt can be earned through repentance. Save for those few who defect to perdition after having known a fulness, there is no habit, no addiction, no rebellion, no transgression, no offense exempted from the promise of complete forgiveness.
Relief from torment and guilt. Those are strong words, and they are meant for people who are really struggling.
Elder Neil L. Andersen added his own witness in the October 2009 general conference, in his talk "Repent . . . That I May Heal You":

I testify that the Savior is able and eager to forgive our sins. Except for the sins of those few who choose perdition after having known a fulness, there is no sin that cannot be forgiven. What a marvelous privilege for each of us to turn away from our sins and to come unto Christ. Divine forgiveness is one of the sweetest fruits of the gospel, removing guilt and pain from our hearts and replacing them with joy and peace of conscience.
A marvelous privilege. Not a burden. Not a sentence. A privilege. If you are still punishing yourself, ask whether you are holding on to something the Savior already took from you.
Here is the last thing I want to say. Forgiveness is something we practice, like a muscle we build.
Peter wanted a limit. He asked the Lord how many times he had to forgive.

Then came Peter to him, and said, Lord, how oft shall my brother sin against me, and I forgive him? till seven times? Jesus saith unto him, I say not unto thee, Until seven times: but, Until seventy times seven.
Seventy times seven is 490. But no one is meant to keep a tally and stop at 491. The Lord is saying the number is not the point. The heart is.
Paul tells us what kind of heart to build.

Let all bitterness, and wrath, and anger, and clamour, and evil speaking, be put away from you, with all malice: And be ye kind one to another, tenderhearted, forgiving one another, even as God for Christ's sake hath forgiven you.
Notice the list of things to put away. Bitterness. Wrath. Anger. Loud words. Evil speaking. Malice. Then notice what takes their place. Kindness. A tender heart. Forgiveness.
You do not do this once. You do it every time the old feeling comes back. And each time, it gets a little easier, and a little quieter.

story.prompt: The member tells a true time when they forgave someone, or when someone forgave them. If the member has none, the app offers a story from the scriptures.
story.title: The unmerciful servant

blocks.text: Jesus told a story about a servant who owed his master a huge amount. The master forgave the whole debt. But then that same servant found a fellow servant who owed him a small amount. He grabbed him and had him thrown in prison. When the master heard, this is what he said.

Then his lord, after that he had called him, said unto him, O thou wicked servant, I forgave thee all that debt, because thou desiredst me: Shouldest not thou also have had compassion on thy fellowservant, even as I had pity on thee? And his lord was wroth, and delivered him to the tormentors, till he should pay all that was due unto him. So likewise shall my heavenly Father do also unto you, if ye from your hearts forgive not every one his brother their trespasses.
The servant had been forgiven a great deal and could not forgive a little. We are that servant when we forget how much we have been forgiven. The story invites us to remember. Then to act.

application.text: Here are three small steps for this week.
First, think of one person you have not forgiven. You do not have to feel ready. Just say their name in a prayer.
Second, ask Heavenly Father for the feeling of forgiveness, the way President Faust taught. Then watch for small chances to be kind. A text. A greeting. A good word about them to someone else.

Third, if you are hard on yourself, read Alma 24:10 and 1 John 1:9 out loud. Let the words do their work. If a heavy sin has not been fully dealt with, speak with your bishop or branch president. That is part of how He lifts it.

testimony.prompt: The member adds their own words. Lines the app offers:

blocks.text: I know that God is merciful. I know that Jesus Christ paid the price so that we could be forgiven. I have seen what happens when a heart finally lets go of a grudge. Peace comes in. I testify that this peace is real and that it is for each of us. In the name of Jesus Christ, amen.

invitations: I invite you to say the name of one person you have not forgiven in prayer.
I invite you to ask Heavenly Father for the feeling of forgiveness and look for small chances to be kind.
I invite you to speak with your bishop or branch president if a heavy sin has not been fully dealt with.
blessings: Your heart will begin to heal.

closingVerse.text: Let the wicked forsake his way, and the unrighteous man his thoughts: and let him return unto the Lord, and he will have mercy upon him; and to our God, for he will abundantly pardon.

opening.text: Picture a man in a small cell. The walls are gray. The bed is hard. He has been there a long time, and he has gotten used to it. He paces. He complains about the guard. He rehearses what he would say to the person who put him there.
One day he leans on the door, and it swings open. It was never locked. The latch was on the inside. All those years, the only thing holding him in was his own hand on the bolt.
Unforgiveness works like that. We think the other person has the key. We wait for an apology, or for them to change, or for them to finally see what they did. And we stay in the cell.
But the Savior tells us something surprising. The door opens from our side. We do not need their permission to walk out.
Today I want to talk about that door. I will share what God has done to forgive us, what He asks of us in return, and how to take that first step into the open air.

mainMessage.text: Forgiveness opens a door that only we can open. Because Jesus Christ forgave us, we can forgive others, and we can find freedom and peace on the other side.

blocks.text: Let's begin by asking what kind of God we are dealing with.
If you grew up thinking of Him as strict and hard to please, the Psalms may surprise you. David sang about the Lord's character this way.

The Lord is merciful and gracious, slow to anger, and plenteous in mercy. He will not always chide: neither will he keep his anger for ever. He hath not dealt with us after our sins; nor rewarded us according to our iniquities. For as the heaven is high above the earth, so great is his mercy toward them that fear him. As far as the east is from the west, so far hath he removed our transgressions from us.
He has not dealt with us after our sins. Think about that. If He gave us exactly what we deserved, none of us would stand. Instead, He is patient. He is merciful. He gives us time.
So what do we do with our sins? John tells us the simple path.
If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.
Confess, and He forgives. And not only forgives. He cleanses. A forgiven person is not just excused. A forgiven person is made clean.
Isaiah gives us one more line to hold on to. It is the Lord speaking directly.
I, even I, am he that blotteth out thy transgressions for mine own sake, and will not remember thy sins.
Blotted out. Think of a page where the ink has been lifted away. Nothing left to read. That is how He deals with a sin we have truly turned from.

I start here because it sets the tone for everything else. Before we are asked to do anything, we are shown what He has already done. His love comes first. His commands follow. That is how a good Father teaches.
Someone might ask, "How can mercy be fair? If God just wipes it away, what about justice?"
That is a fair question, and the gospel has an answer. Justice was satisfied by Jesus Christ. He did not ignore the debt. He paid it.
In whom we have redemption through his blood, even the forgiveness of sins.
In Gethsemane, He took our sins upon Himself. On the cross, He gave His life. That is the price of the door that is open to us. We did not earn it. We could not.
And because of that price, the offer does not run out. The Lord said to Alma:
Yea, and as often as my people repent will I forgive them their trespasses against me.
As often as. If you have been through the same struggle a dozen times, that promise is for you. Each time you turn back, the answer is the same.
Elder Russell M. Nelson helped many of us see forgiveness in a fresh way. In his talk "The Atonement," from the October 1996 general conference, he taught:

Rich meaning is found in study of the word atonement in the Semitic languages of Old Testament times. In Hebrew, the basic word for atonement is kaphar, a verb that means “to cover” or “to forgive.” Closely related is the Aramaic and Arabic word kafat, meaning “a close embrace”—no doubt related to the Egyptian ritual embrace. References to that embrace are evident in the Book of Mormon. One states that “the Lord hath redeemed my soul . . . ; I have beheld his glory, and I am encircled about eternally in the arms of his love.” \[2 Nephi 1:15.\] Another proffers the glorious hope of our being “clasped in the arms of Jesus.” \[Mormon 5:11.\]
A close embrace. Think about the difference between being pardoned by a stranger and being hugged by someone who loves you. The Atonement is the second one.
Lehi felt this when he blessed his family.
But behold, the Lord hath redeemed my soul from hell; I have beheld his glory, and I am encircled about eternally in the arms of his love.
So when we step out of the cell, we are not stepping into an empty field. We are stepping into the arms of the One who made the way.
Now, the door. How does it open?
It opens when we choose to forgive. And the Lord does not leave us guessing about this choice. He taught it in the Sermon on the Mount.
For if ye forgive men their trespasses, your heavenly Father will also forgive you: But if ye forgive not men their trespasses, neither will your Father forgive your trespasses.

When I first read that, I felt a little worried. It sounded like a trade. But the more I think about it, the more I see it as a description. The unforgiving heart is a closed heart. And a closed heart cannot receive.
In our time, He gave a similar teaching to the Saints.

Wherefore, I say unto you, that ye ought to forgive one another; for he that forgiveth not his brother his trespasses standeth condemned before the Lord; for there remaineth in him the greater sin. I, the Lord, will forgive whom I will forgive, but of you it is required to forgive all men. And ye ought to say in your hearts—let God judge between me and thee, and reward thee according to thy deeds.

Let God judge between me and thee. I find real relief in that sentence. I am not asked to prove anything. I am not asked to settle the score. I am asked to step back and let a perfectly fair Judge handle what I cannot.
The Lord knows how hard this is. So did President Gordon B. Hinckley. In his article "Of You It Is Required to Forgive," in the June 1991 Ensign, he wrote:
I plead with you to ask the Lord for strength to forgive. . . . It may not be easy, and it may not come quickly. But if you will seek it with sincerity and cultivate it, it will come.
Ask for strength. Seek it sincerely. Keep at it. That is a path anyone can walk, even on a day when the anger is loud.
So you are standing at the door. What does it take to push it open?
It starts with being honest. You cannot leave a cell you pretend is not there. If you are angry, say so, at least to yourself and to God.
President James E. Faust taught this in his April 2007 general conference talk, "The Healing Power of Forgiveness." He said:

We need to recognize and acknowledge angry feelings. It will take humility to do this, but if we will get on our knees and ask Heavenly Father for a feeling of forgiveness, He will help us. The Lord requires us “to forgive all men” \[D&C 64:10\] for our own good because “hatred retards spiritual growth.” \[Orson F. Whitney, Gospel Themes (1914), 144.\] Only as we rid ourselves of hatred and bitterness can the Lord put comfort into our hearts. . . .
For our own good. I want you to hear that. When the Lord asks us to forgive, He is thinking of us. Hatred slows down our growth. Letting it go lets us move.
Next, we look at how Christ handled it. Paul says:
Forbearing one another, and forgiving one another, if any man have a quarrel against any: even as Christ forgave you, so also do ye.
So also do ye. We are given the same job He had, in smaller form. We forgive, as He forgave.
Then comes the part about judging. Jesus said:
Judge not, and ye shall not be judged: condemn not, and ye shall not be condemned: forgive, and ye shall be forgiven.
This is not telling us to have no standards. It is telling us not to take the seat that belongs to God.
And then, the cross.
Then said Jesus, Father, forgive them; for they know not what they do. And they parted his raiment, and cast lots.
That is the example I go back to when my own heart is slow. If He could say that, then surely I can ask for help to say something like it.
President Faust also gave a caution for deep wounds.

. . . When tragedy strikes, we should not respond by seeking personal revenge but rather let justice take its course and then let go. It is not easy to let go and empty our hearts of festering resentment. The Savior has offered to all of us a precious peace through His Atonement, but this can come only as we are willing to cast out negative feelings of anger, spite, or revenge.
He is honest. It is not easy. But he also points to the reward, a precious peace. And that peace comes through the Atonement.
There is another cell some of us live in. It is the one we built for ourselves.
We know what we did. We have repented. But we keep going back to the memory, as if serving more time will somehow make up for it.
The Lord never asked us to serve extra time. Look at what happened with the people of Ammon. They were Lamanites who had done terrible things. After their conversion, their king prayed:

And I also thank my God, yea, my great God, that he hath granted unto us that we might repent of these things, and also that he hath forgiven us of those our many sins and murders which we have committed, and taken away the guilt from our hearts, through the merits of his Son.
Through the merits of His Son. Not through their own long suffering. The guilt was taken away because of Jesus Christ.
President Boyd K. Packer said this about the reach of the promise. In his October 1995 general conference talk, "The Brilliant Morning of Forgiveness," he taught:

The gospel teaches us that relief from torment and guilt can be earned through repentance. Save for those few who defect to perdition after having known a fulness, there is no habit, no addiction, no rebellion, no transgression, no offense exempted from the promise of complete forgiveness.
When I read this, I notice the word complete. Not partial. Not probationary. Complete.
Elder Neil L. Andersen bore the same witness in October 2009, in his talk "Repent . . . That I May Heal You":

I testify that the Savior is able and eager to forgive our sins. Except for the sins of those few who choose perdition after having known a fulness, there is no sin that cannot be forgiven. What a marvelous privilege for each of us to turn away from our sins and to come unto Christ. Divine forgiveness is one of the sweetest fruits of the gospel, removing guilt and pain from our hearts and replacing them with joy and peace of conscience.
Joy and peace of conscience. That is what is waiting on the other side of the door. If you have been standing in that cell a long time, please try the door.
One last thing. The door does not stay open on its own. We have to keep walking out.
Peter once asked the Savior how far this goes.

Then came Peter to him, and said, Lord, how oft shall my brother sin against me, and I forgive him? till seven times? Jesus saith unto him, I say not unto thee, Until seven times: but, Until seventy times seven.
The Savior did not give Peter a new number to count. He gave him a new way to live. Forgiveness becomes a habit of the heart.
And Paul describes what that habit looks like.

Let all bitterness, and wrath, and anger, and clamour, and evil speaking, be put away from you, with all malice: And be ye kind one to another, tenderhearted, forgiving one another, even as God for Christ's sake hath forgiven you.
It is a very practical list. Put away bitterness. Put away loud arguments and cutting remarks. Choose kindness. Choose a soft heart.
Some days it will feel like you have walked back into the cell. That is normal. Keep going. Each time you choose the open air, it gets a little more natural.

story.prompt: The member tells a true time when they forgave someone, or when someone forgave them. If the member has none, the app offers a story from the scriptures.
story.title: Stephen forgives those who stoned him

blocks.text: Stephen was a faithful disciple who taught about Jesus. A crowd grew furious and dragged him out of the city to stone him. As the stones struck, he did not curse them. This is what the record says.

And they stoned Stephen, calling upon God, and saying, Lord Jesus, receive my spirit. And he kneeled down, and cried with a loud voice, Lord, lay not this sin to their charge. And when he had said this, he fell asleep.
He was dying, and his last prayer was for the people who were killing him. He learned that from the Savior. Stephen was free, even as the stones fell. No wall could hold him.

application.text: Try this over the next week.

Sit down and ask yourself where the door is. Which hurt do you keep going back to? Name it. Then say a short prayer: "Heavenly Father, help me want to forgive." That is a real prayer, and He will answer it.
Next, do one small thing that moves you toward open air. Say a kind word. Skip a bitter reply. Pray for the person who hurt you.

If you are the one who is carrying guilt, do not stay in your own cell. Read 1 John 1:9. Confess to the Lord. If the matter needs it, talk with your bishop or branch president. Then believe the Lord when He says you are cleansed.

blocks.text: I know that the door is open. Jesus Christ opened it for us, at a great price. I have felt the peace that comes when I choose to forgive. I know it is not always quick, but it is always worth it. I bear this witness in the name of Jesus Christ, amen.

invitations: I invite you to name the hurt you keep going back to.
I invite you to pray, "Heavenly Father, help me want to forgive."
I invite you to confess to the Lord, and talk with your bishop or branch president if the matter needs it.

closingVerse.text:
And it came to pass that as I was thus racked with torment, while I was harrowed up by the memory of my many sins, behold, I remembered also to have heard my father prophesy unto the people concerning the coming of one Jesus Christ, a Son of God, to atone for the sins of the world.
Now, as my mind caught hold upon this thought, I cried within my heart: O Jesus, thou Son of God, have mercy on me, who am in the gall of bitterness, and am encircled about by the everlasting chains of death.
And now, behold, when I thought this, I could remember my pains no more; yea, I was harrowed up by the memory of my sins no more.

opening.text: Think about a river. It starts high in the mountains, and the water runs freely down to the valley. Farms are watered. Towns grow. Fish swim. Life follows it.

Now imagine someone builds a dam across that river. At first nothing seems wrong. The water backs up, and a lake forms. But downstream, the riverbed dries out. The fields turn brown. And behind the dam, the pressure keeps rising.

A heart can be a dam. When someone hurts us, we sometimes build a wall to hold back everything: the trust, the warmth, the kindness. We call it protection. And for a short time, it may be. But if we leave the wall up for years, the life we meant to protect starts to dry out. Our friendships thin. Our joy gets smaller. And the pressure behind the wall keeps growing.
Forgiveness opens the gate. It lets the water move again. It does not wash away what happened, but it lets life flow back.
Today I will talk about the source of that water. It begins with the Savior. We will look at how He forgives us, why He asks us to forgive others, and how we can open our own gates.

mainMessage.text: The Savior's forgiveness flows to us, and it is meant to flow through us. When we forgive, the water of peace moves again, first in our own hearts and then in the lives around us.

blocks.text: The source of all of this is God's own heart. So let's begin there.
If you are not sure what kind of Being He is, listen to David's song.

The Lord is merciful and gracious, slow to anger, and plenteous in mercy. He will not always chide: neither will he keep his anger for ever. He hath not dealt with us after our sins; nor rewarded us according to our iniquities. For as the heaven is high above the earth, so great is his mercy toward them that fear him. As far as the east is from the west, so far hath he removed our transgressions from us.
Slow to anger. Plenteous in mercy. These are not words of someone who is looking for a reason to punish. They are the words of someone who is looking for a reason to forgive.
How does that mercy reach us? Through honest confession.
If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.
There is no maze to walk through. If we confess, He forgives. He is faithful, and He keeps His word every time.
Here is what He says about what happens to the sin after.
I, even I, am he that blotteth out thy transgressions for mine own sake, and will not remember thy sins.
For mine own sake. That is a tender phrase. God forgives because of who He is. It comes from His nature. It is who He is. He wants us whole.
So the water starts at His heart. It is clean, and there is plenty of it.
But how did it get from His heart to ours? It came through a channel that cost Him dearly.
The channel is the Atonement of Jesus Christ. Paul calls it redemption.
In whom we have redemption through his blood, even the forgiveness of sins.

Through His blood. That phrase reminds us of the price. It was not a quiet, easy thing. It was suffering beyond what we can picture. And He did it willingly, so that forgiveness could flow to every one of us.
The Book of Mormon tells us the supply does not run dry.
Yea, and as often as my people repent will I forgive them their trespasses against me.
As often as. We might worry that we are using up the supply. We are not. This river does not run out.
In October 1996, Elder Russell M. Nelson gave a talk called "The Atonement." He pointed to the ancient meaning behind the word. He said:

Rich meaning is found in study of the word atonement in the Semitic languages of Old Testament times. In Hebrew, the basic word for atonement is kaphar, a verb that means “to cover” or “to forgive.” Closely related is the Aramaic and Arabic word kafat, meaning “a close embrace”—no doubt related to the Egyptian ritual embrace. References to that embrace are evident in the Book of Mormon. One states that “the Lord hath redeemed my soul . . . ; I have beheld his glory, and I am encircled about eternally in the arms of his love.” \[2 Nephi 1:15.\] Another proffers the glorious hope of our being “clasped in the arms of Jesus.” \[Mormon 5:11.\]
Covered. Embraced. Encircled. Those are words about closeness. The Atonement does more than clear a debt. It brings us near.
Lehi said it in his own words.
But behold, the Lord hath redeemed my soul from hell; I have beheld his glory, and I am encircled about eternally in the arms of his love.
When we feel that love, we want to share it. And that is why the next step makes sense.
The water was never meant to stop with us. It is meant to flow on.
The Savior taught it directly.
For if ye forgive men their trespasses, your heavenly Father will also forgive you: But if ye forgive not men their trespasses, neither will your Father forgive your trespasses.

Think of the dam. If I block the river downstream, what happens upstream? The water has nowhere to go. In the same way, when I refuse to let mercy pass through me, I also stop receiving it. This is a description of how a heart works. A blocked heart cannot take in what a flowing heart can.
The Lord restated this in our day.

Wherefore, I say unto you, that ye ought to forgive one another; for he that forgiveth not his brother his trespasses standeth condemned before the Lord; for there remaineth in him the greater sin. I, the Lord, will forgive whom I will forgive, but of you it is required to forgive all men. And ye ought to say in your hearts—let God judge between me and thee, and reward thee according to thy deeds.
The last line is the key to opening the gate. Say it in your heart. Let God judge. The weight of judging is not ours. The Lord takes it, and we are free to let the water move.
President Gordon B. Hinckley was a very kind and practical man. In his article "Of You It Is Required to Forgive," in the June 1991 Ensign, he wrote:
I plead with you to ask the Lord for strength to forgive. . . . It may not be easy, and it may not come quickly. But if you will seek it with sincerity and cultivate it, it will come.
A gate that has been closed for years may be stiff. It may take some effort, and some time. But he promises that if we keep seeking, it will come.
How do we open the gate? Let's go step by step.
The first step is to look at the wall honestly. What are we holding back, and why? Often it is anger. Sometimes it is fear. Sometimes it is pain we do not want to feel again.
President James E. Faust gave good counsel in his talk "The Healing Power of Forgiveness," from the April 2007 general conference. He said:

We need to recognize and acknowledge angry feelings. It will take humility to do this, but if we will get on our knees and ask Heavenly Father for a feeling of forgiveness, He will help us. The Lord requires us “to forgive all men” \[D&C 64:10\] for our own good because “hatred retards spiritual growth.” \[Orson F. Whitney, Gospel Themes (1914), 144.\] Only as we rid ourselves of hatred and bitterness can the Lord put comfort into our hearts. . . .
See how it works. Acknowledge. Kneel. Ask. Then the Lord does what we cannot, and He puts comfort into our hearts. We do not have to force the gate open by ourselves.
The second step is to remember our model. Paul wrote:
Forbearing one another, and forgiving one another, if any man have a quarrel against any: even as Christ forgave you, so also do ye.
If Christ is the pattern, then we know the shape of it. Generous. Patient. Willing to go first.
The third step is to put down the gavel. This is the hardest for many of us. We want to be the ones who decide what the other person deserves. But Jesus said:
Judge not, and ye shall not be judged: condemn not, and ye shall not be condemned: forgive, and ye shall be forgiven.
Then He lived it.
Then said Jesus, Father, forgive them; for they know not what they do. And they parted his raiment, and cast lots.
He did not wait until the soldiers understood. He forgave while they were still at it.
What about when the wrong was truly serious? President Faust said:

. . . When tragedy strikes, we should not respond by seeking personal revenge but rather let justice take its course and then let go. It is not easy to let go and empty our hearts of festering resentment. The Savior has offered to all of us a precious peace through His Atonement, but this can come only as we are willing to cast out negative feelings of anger, spite, or revenge.

He separates two things. Justice is one thing. Resentment is another. We can let the law, our leaders, and God deal with justice. And we can set our own hearts free from resentment. The first does not require the second.
Now let's turn the river toward ourselves.
Some people let mercy flow to others, but they put a dam up against themselves. They say, "I will forgive anyone but me."
The scriptures do not support that wall. Listen to what the king of the Lamanites, who had murdered and fought against the Nephites, prayed after he was converted.

And I also thank my God, yea, my great God, that he hath granted unto us that we might repent of these things, and also that he hath forgiven us of those our many sins and murders which we have committed, and taken away the guilt from our hearts, through the merits of his Son.
The guilt was taken away. That is the result when mercy flows all the way in. It does not leave a trace of shame that we have to carry for years.
President Boyd K. Packer explained how wide the promise is in his October 1995 general conference talk, "The Brilliant Morning of Forgiveness." He said:

The gospel teaches us that relief from torment and guilt can be earned through repentance. Save for those few who defect to perdition after having known a fulness, there is no habit, no addiction, no rebellion, no transgression, no offense exempted from the promise of complete forgiveness.
The word torment is honest. Guilt can be torture. But he says relief is available, and complete forgiveness is promised.
Elder Neil L. Andersen gave his own witness in the October 2009 general conference, in his talk "Repent . . . That I May Heal You":

I testify that the Savior is able and eager to forgive our sins. Except for the sins of those few who choose perdition after having known a fulness, there is no sin that cannot be forgiven. What a marvelous privilege for each of us to turn away from our sins and to come unto Christ. Divine forgiveness is one of the sweetest fruits of the gospel, removing guilt and pain from our hearts and replacing them with joy and peace of conscience.
Joy and peace of conscience. If you have been holding back the water for years, let it come. It is meant for you too.
A river does not flow once. It flows every day. And forgiveness is the same.
Peter wanted to know where the limit was.

Then came Peter to him, and said, Lord, how oft shall my brother sin against me, and I forgive him? till seven times? Jesus saith unto him, I say not unto thee, Until seven times: but, Until seventy times seven.
The Savior's answer takes away the limit. We do not forgive once and then stop. We keep the gate open.
And Paul tells us what that looks like in plain terms.

Let all bitterness, and wrath, and anger, and clamour, and evil speaking, be put away from you, with all malice: And be ye kind one to another, tenderhearted, forgiving one another, even as God for Christ's sake hath forgiven you.

Notice that kindness and tenderheartedness go together with forgiveness. We cannot clear the bitterness and leave a blank space. We have to fill the space with something good. Kind words. Soft eyes. A willingness to start fresh.
That is how the riverbed turns green again.

story.prompt: The member tells a true time when they forgave someone, or when someone forgave them. If the member has none, the app offers a story from the scriptures.
story.title: Jacob and Esau meet again

blocks.text: Years before, Jacob had taken his brother Esau's birthright and blessing, and Esau had wanted to kill him. Jacob ran away. Twenty years later, Jacob came home with his family. He was terrified. He sent gifts ahead. He bowed to the ground seven times as he came near. And this is what happened.
And Esau ran to meet him, and embraced him, and fell on his neck, and kissed him: and they wept.

Esau ran. He did not walk slowly, waiting for Jacob to make the first move. Twenty years of wall came down in a moment. They wept together. The gate had been open in Esau's heart longer than Jacob knew.

application.text: Here is a simple plan for this week.
Spend a few minutes thinking about where the water has stopped in your life. A relationship that went quiet. A person you avoid. A memory you keep behind a wall.
Then choose one small way to open the gate. You do not have to reach out to the person if it would not be safe. You can start in prayer. Ask Heavenly Father to soften your heart.
If you carry guilt over something you did, let the mercy flow to you. Read Alma 24:10 and 1 John 1:9. If it is a heavy matter, speak with your bishop or branch president. They are there to help.

testimony.prompt: The member adds their own words. Lines the app offers:

blocks.text: I know that the Savior's mercy is real and that it flows freely. I know that when I forgive, something in me gets quiet and clear. I have seen it in my own life and in others. I know that Jesus Christ is the source of that peace. I say this in the name of Jesus Christ, amen.

invitations: I invite you to think about where the water has stopped in your life.
I invite you to ask Heavenly Father to soften your heart.
I invite you to speak with your bishop or branch president if you carry guilt over something heavy.

closingVerse.text: He that covereth his sins shall not prosper: but whoso confesseth and forsaketh them shall have mercy.

opening.text: Some years ago, a town lost its bridge to a flood. The river was wide, and for a while the two sides of town were cut off from each other. People who lived a few hundred yards apart could not visit. Children could not reach the school. A shop on one bank lost its customers on the other.
It did not take long for people to feel how much they had depended on that one bridge. Without it, everything got harder.

A grudge does the same thing between two people. At first, it is a small crack. Then the flood comes. A harsh word. A broken promise. A long silence. And the bridge is gone. Two people who once sat at the same table now live on opposite banks.
Forgiveness is the work of rebuilding. It is slow, and it asks something of both sides. But it starts with one person laying the first plank.
Today I want to talk about how Jesus Christ rebuilt the bridge between us and God, and how He invites us to rebuild the bridges between us and each other.

mainMessage.text: Jesus Christ built the bridge between us and God, and He asks us to build bridges to one another. When we forgive, we reconnect, and we find healing that we could not give ourselves.

blocks.text: Let's start at the first bridge. The one between us and our Heavenly Father.
We sometimes assume that bridge is gone. We think our mistakes have washed it out, and that He is waiting on the far bank with folded arms. The scriptures say that is not so.

The Lord is merciful and gracious, slow to anger, and plenteous in mercy. He will not always chide: neither will he keep his anger for ever. He hath not dealt with us after our sins; nor rewarded us according to our iniquities. For as the heaven is high above the earth, so great is his mercy toward them that fear him. As far as the east is from the west, so far hath he removed our transgressions from us.
He is not on the far bank with folded arms. He is slow to anger. He is full of mercy. He has not treated us as our sins deserve.
So how do we cross? John gives us the plain answer.
If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.
Confession is the first step onto the bridge. We say what is true. And He is faithful. He meets us there.
Then Isaiah gives us a promise in the Lord's own words.
I, even I, am he that blotteth out thy transgressions for mine own sake, and will not remember thy sins.

That is something we cannot do for each other. People remember. They bring it up at the next argument. But God says, I will not remember. Once we have crossed, He does not drag the old flood back into the room.
Who built this bridge? It was Jesus Christ.

We could not have built it. No amount of apology or effort on our side could span that distance. So He did it. He took the weight of our sins. He bled in Gethsemane. He gave His life on the cross. Paul writes:
In whom we have redemption through his blood, even the forgiveness of sins.
The bridge is made of His sacrifice. Every time we cross, we are walking on something that cost Him greatly.
And the bridge is always open. The Lord told Alma:
Yea, and as often as my people repent will I forgive them their trespasses against me.
No toll. No limit on the number of crossings. As often as we repent, we are welcomed back.
Elder Russell M. Nelson, in his October 1996 general conference talk "The Atonement," said something that helped me see what is waiting on the other side:

Rich meaning is found in study of the word atonement in the Semitic languages of Old Testament times. In Hebrew, the basic word for atonement is kaphar, a verb that means “to cover” or “to forgive.” Closely related is the Aramaic and Arabic word kafat, meaning “a close embrace”—no doubt related to the Egyptian ritual embrace. References to that embrace are evident in the Book of Mormon. One states that “the Lord hath redeemed my soul . . . ; I have beheld his glory, and I am encircled about eternally in the arms of his love.” \[2 Nephi 1:15.\] Another proffers the glorious hope of our being “clasped in the arms of Jesus.” \[Mormon 5:11.\]
A bridge leads somewhere. This one leads to an embrace. When we cross, we are not met with a lecture. We are met with open arms.
Lehi described it that way.
But behold, the Lord hath redeemed my soul from hell; I have beheld his glory, and I am encircled about eternally in the arms of his love.
It is hard to stay angry at the world when you have been held like that.
Now think of the other bridges in your life. The ones between you and the people who have hurt you.
The Savior does not ask us to build these alone. But He does ask us to lay the first plank, even when we feel it should be the other person's job. He said:
For if ye forgive men their trespasses, your heavenly Father will also forgive you: But if ye forgive not men their trespasses, neither will your Father forgive your trespasses.

I used to hear this as a threat. Now I hear it as a pattern. The way we deal with others is the way we learn to receive from God. A person who burns every bridge will find it hard to believe any bridge is open to them.
The Lord spoke again to the early Saints and said:

Wherefore, I say unto you, that ye ought to forgive one another; for he that forgiveth not his brother his trespasses standeth condemned before the Lord; for there remaineth in him the greater sin. I, the Lord, will forgive whom I will forgive, but of you it is required to forgive all men. And ye ought to say in your hearts—let God judge between me and thee, and reward thee according to thy deeds.
Of you it is required. That is firm. But look at the instruction in the last line. Say it in your heart. Let God judge. He holds the scales. We hold the plank.
President Gordon B. Hinckley understood how difficult this can be. In his article "Of You It Is Required to Forgive," in the June 1991 Ensign, he wrote:
I plead with you to ask the Lord for strength to forgive. . . . It may not be easy, and it may not come quickly. But if you will seek it with sincerity and cultivate it, it will come.
A bridge takes time. You do not need to finish it today. You only need to start and ask for strength.
So how do we lay the first plank? Here is where the practical help comes in.
We start by telling the truth about what we feel. A bridge cannot be built over a river we pretend is not there.
President James E. Faust gave this counsel in his talk "The Healing Power of Forgiveness," from the April 2007 general conference:

We need to recognize and acknowledge angry feelings. It will take humility to do this, but if we will get on our knees and ask Heavenly Father for a feeling of forgiveness, He will help us. The Lord requires us “to forgive all men” \[D&C 64:10\] for our own good because “hatred retards spiritual growth.” \[Orson F. Whitney, Gospel Themes (1914), 144.\] Only as we rid ourselves of hatred and bitterness can the Lord put comfort into our hearts. . . .
See the invitation. Kneel. Ask Heavenly Father for a feeling of forgiveness. If you are not there yet, ask for the wish to get there. He will help us.
Next, we need the right blueprint. Paul gave it in one line.
Forbearing one another, and forgiving one another, if any man have a quarrel against any: even as Christ forgave you, so also do ye.
Even as Christ forgave you. His way is the design for every bridge we build.
We also need to leave the work of judging to the right person. Jesus said:
Judge not, and ye shall not be judged: condemn not, and ye shall not be condemned: forgive, and ye shall be forgiven.
This frees us from having to figure out what the other person deserves. We can build without deciding who was more at fault.
And on the cross, He showed us the strongest bridge of all.
Then said Jesus, Father, forgive them; for they know not what they do. And they parted his raiment, and cast lots.
He started the bridge from His side, in the middle of His pain.
President Faust wrote something that helps when the wound is serious.

. . . When tragedy strikes, we should not respond by seeking personal revenge but rather let justice take its course and then let go. It is not easy to let go and empty our hearts of festering resentment. The Savior has offered to all of us a precious peace through His Atonement, but this can come only as we are willing to cast out negative feelings of anger, spite, or revenge.

Some bridges should not be rebuilt the same way. If someone has put you in danger, forgiving them does not mean going back into harm. It means releasing the anger and trusting God and righteous justice to handle the rest. You can forgive and still keep a safe distance.
There is one more bridge, and it is the one many of us forget. It is the bridge between who we were and who we are becoming.
Some of us stand on one side, looking back at our worst moments, and refuse to cross. We say, "I am still that person." But the Savior says we do not have to stay.
The Lamanite king who was converted by Ammon's teaching said it clearly in his prayer.

And I also thank my God, yea, my great God, that he hath granted unto us that we might repent of these things, and also that he hath forgiven us of those our many sins and murders which we have committed, and taken away the guilt from our hearts, through the merits of his Son.
He had been a man of war. He crossed. And on the other side, the guilt was gone.
President Boyd K. Packer taught about the promise in his talk "The Brilliant Morning of Forgiveness," from the October 1995 general conference:

The gospel teaches us that relief from torment and guilt can be earned through repentance. Save for those few who defect to perdition after having known a fulness, there is no habit, no addiction, no rebellion, no transgression, no offense exempted from the promise of complete forgiveness.
The key word is exempted. Nothing on your list is left out of the promise.
Elder Neil L. Andersen bore a similar testimony in his talk "Repent . . . That I May Heal You," from the October 2009 general conference:

I testify that the Savior is able and eager to forgive our sins. Except for the sins of those few who choose perdition after having known a fulness, there is no sin that cannot be forgiven. What a marvelous privilege for each of us to turn away from our sins and to come unto Christ. Divine forgiveness is one of the sweetest fruits of the gospel, removing guilt and pain from our hearts and replacing them with joy and peace of conscience.
Eager. The Savior is waiting at the other end of the bridge, and He is not looking at His watch.
Bridges need upkeep. We have to keep walking across them, and we have to keep repairing them.
Peter once asked the Savior how often to forgive.

Then came Peter to him, and said, Lord, how oft shall my brother sin against me, and I forgive him? till seven times? Jesus saith unto him, I say not unto thee, Until seven times: but, Until seventy times seven.
The answer was not a number to track. It was a way of living. We keep repairing the bridge, plank by plank.
Paul tells us what the repairs look like.

Let all bitterness, and wrath, and anger, and clamour, and evil speaking, be put away from you, with all malice: And be ye kind one to another, tenderhearted, forgiving one another, even as God for Christ's sake hath forgiven you.
Put away the things that damage. Choose the things that connect. A kind word is a plank. A patient answer is a plank. A short prayer for someone who is hard to love is a plank.
One by one, they add up. And one day you look up and realize you can walk across.

story.prompt: The member tells a true time when they forgave someone, or when someone forgave them. If the member has none, the app offers a story from the scriptures.
story.title: The woman who anointed Jesus

blocks.text: Jesus was a guest at the home of a man named Simon. A woman known in town for her sins came in. She wept at the Savior's feet, wiped them with her hair, and anointed them. Simon judged her silently. Jesus turned and spoke.
Wherefore I say unto thee, Her sins, which are many, are forgiven; for she loved much: but to whom little is forgiven, the same loveth little. And he said unto her, Thy sins are forgiven.

She crossed a very hard bridge that day. She walked into a room full of people who judged her. And she met the One who forgave her. Her love came from the weight she had been relieved of. Jesus said, "Thy sins are forgiven." She heard it from Him directly.

application.text: Try these three things this week.
Pick one bridge to repair. It might be a person who hurt you. It might be a friendship that has gone cold. It might be your own heart. You do not need to cross all the way. Just lay one plank.
Pray each day for the feeling of forgiveness. Keep it short. "Heavenly Father, help me forgive." That is enough.
And if guilt is the thing between you and Him, go and talk with Him honestly. Read 1 John 1:9. If it is a serious matter, talk to your bishop or branch president. They will help you cross.

testimony.prompt: The member adds their own words. Lines the app offers:

blocks.text: I know that Jesus Christ has made a way for us to come home. I know that He forgives, and I know that He gives us the strength to forgive others. I have felt His mercy in my own life, and I am grateful. I say these things in the name of Jesus Christ, amen.

invitations: I invite you to pick one bridge to repair and lay one plank this week.
I invite you to pray each day, "Heavenly Father, help me forgive."
I invite you to talk with your bishop or branch president if guilt stands between you and Him.
blessings: You will be able to cross.

closingVerse.text: Repent ye therefore, and be converted, that your sins may be blotted out, when the times of refreshing shall come from the presence of the Lord;
